nodes.name: Three-term irrational AP
nodes.statement: The first example could have been analysed by Davenport and Heilbronn using the methods of , but we include it here to demonstrate the simplest case in which Corollary applies. Let L := Big( 1 & -sqrt2 & -1 + sqrt 2Big). Then m=1 and d=3, and manifestly there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of L that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates. Therefore Corollary applies, and so, if for each N we have three functions f_1,f_2,f_3:[N] longrightarrow [-1,1] satisfying min_j Vert f_jVert_U^2[N] leqslant rho for some rho in the range 0 < rho leqslant 1, then we have Bigvertfrac1N^2sumlimits_substackn_1,n_2,n_3leqslant N\\ vert n_1 - sqrt2n_2 + (-1+sqrt2)n_3vertleqslant varepsilon f_1(n_1)f_2(n_2)f_3(n_3)Bigvert ll_varepsilon rho^Omega(1) +o_rho(1) as Nrightarrow infty. The statement () admits a different interpretation, which some readers may find more natural, that of counting the number of occurrences of a certain irrational pattern: a `three-term irrational arithmetic progression'. Indeed, recall that for theta in R we let [theta] denote lfloor theta +frac12rfloor, i.e. the nearest integer to theta. nodes.statement: It may be instructive to consider a matrix such as L = left( 1 +N^-1& sqrt3+N^-frac12 & pi & -pi+sqrt2 \\ 2 & 2sqrt3+N^-frac12 & -sqrt5 & e right). We observe that L has rank 2 and Lnotin V_degen^*(2,4). If one knew Theorem and the conditions (), then one might perhaps have hoped to apply the theory of Gowers norms to bound the number of solutions to inequalities given by L. However, by considering perturbations of the first two columns, we see that dist(L,V_degen^*(2,4))=o(1) as Nrightarrow infty. Indeed, one may perturb L by O(N^-1/2) such that there is a vector (0,0,x_3,x_4) in the row space. So, despite the fact that L is non-degenerate from the point of view of equations, L is degenerate from the point of view of inequalities and the conditions (). Thus, our main theorem on inequalities will not apply to this L. Furthermore, we have another result (Theorem below) which shows that one cannot possibly use Gowers norms to control inequalities given by such an L. Therefore, whatever methods we use to prove Theorem , these methods must necessarily break down when applied to this example.\\

nodes.name: Rank matrix
nodes.statement: Let m,d be natural numbers, with dgeqslant m+1. Let c,C be positive constants. Then there are positive constants D_c,C, D^prime_c,C for which the following holds. nodes.statement: Let m,n be natural numbers, and let (psi_1,dots,psi_m) = Psi:R^nlongrightarrow R^m be a system of homogeneous linear forms. Let iin [m]. We say that Psi is in normal form with respect to psi_i if there exists a non-negative integer s and a collection J_i subseteq \ e_1,dots,e_n\ of the standard basis vectors, satisfying vert J_ivert = s+1, such that prodlimits_ein J_i psi_i^prime(e) is non-zero when i^prime = i and vanishes otherwise. We say that Psi is in normal form if it is in normal form with respect to psi_i for every i.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{Definition normal form}
Let $m,n$ be natural numbers, and let $(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_m) = \Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a system of homogeneous linear forms. Let $i\in [m]$. We say that $\Psi$ is in normal form with respect to $\psi_i$ if there exists a non-negative integer $s$ and a collection $J_i \subseteq \{ \mathbf{e_1},\dots,\mathbf{e_n}\}$ of the standard basis vectors, satisfying $\vert J_i\vert = s+1$, such that $$\prod\limits_{\mathbf{e}\in J_i} \psi_{i^\prime}(\mathbf{e})$$ is non-zero when $i^\prime = i$ and vanishes otherwise. We say that $\Psi$ is in normal form if it is in normal form with respect to $\psi_i$ for every $i$.

We say that Psi is in normal form if it is in normal form with respect to psi_i for every i.

nodes.statement: Let m,n be natural numbers, with mgeqslant 2, and let (psi_1,dots,psi_m) = Psi:R^n longrightarrow R^m be a system of homogeneous linear forms. Fix iin [m]. Let P_i be a partition of [m]setminus \i\, i.e. [m]setminus \i\ = bigcuplimits_k=1^s+1 C_k for some s satisfying 0leqslant s leqslant m-2 and some disjoint sets C_k. nodes.raw_latex:
\label{Definition suitable partitions}
Let $m,n$ be natural numbers, with $m\geqslant 2$, and let $(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_m) = \Psi:\mathbb{R}^n \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a system of homogeneous linear forms. Fix $i\in [m]$. Let $\mathcal{P}_i$ be a partition of $[m]\setminus \{i\}$, i.e. $$[m]\setminus \{i\} = \bigcup\limits_{k=1}^{s+1} \mathcal{C}_k$$ for some $s$ satisfying $0\leqslant s \leqslant m-2$ and some disjoint sets $\mathcal{C}_k$. We say that $\mathcal{P}_i$ is \emph{suitable} for $\Psi$ if $$\psi_i \notin \operatorname{span}_\mathbb{R}(\psi_j: j\in \mathcal{C}_k)$$ for any $k$.

nodes.statement: Let m,d be natural numbers with d geqslant m+2, and let L:R^d longrightarrow R^m be a surjective linear map. Let Psi: R^d-m longrightarrow R^d be any system of homogeneous linear forms whose image is ker L. Then L in V_degen^*(m,d) if and only if Psi in V_degen(d-m,d).
assumptions: Let m,d be natural numbers with d geqslant m+2, and let L:R^d longrightarrow R^m be a surjective linear map.

conclusions: Then L in V_degen^*(m,d) if and only if Psi in V_degen(d-m,d).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{Proposition easy degeneracy relation}
Let $m,d$ be natural numbers with $d \geqslant m+2$, and let $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map. Let $\Psi: \mathbb{R}^{d-m} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ be any system of homogeneous linear forms whose image is $\ker L$. Then $L \in V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d)$ if and only if $\Psi \in V_{\operatorname{degen}}(d-m,d).$

nodes.statement: In , the simple algorithm that constructs normal form extensions with respect to a fixed i may easily be iterated, and so the authors work with systems that are in normal form with respect to every index i. A careful analysis of the proof in Appendix C of demonstrates that it is sufficient for Psi merely to admit, for each i separately, an extension that is in normal form with respect to psi_i, but this is of little consequence in . Yet certain quantitative aspects of the iteration of the normal form algorithm, critical to our application of these ideas, are not immediately clear to us. We have stated Proposition for normal forms only with respect to a single i, in order to avoid this technical annoyance. \\

Firstly, recall that in our language, the non-degeneracy condition in the statement of Theorem 1.8 of is exactly the condition that Snotin V^*_degen(m,d). One then follows the same linear algebraic reductions as those used in Section 4 of to reduce Theorem 1.8 to Theorem 7.1 of the same paper (the Generalised von Neumann Theorem). Theorem 7.1 may then be considered solely in the case of bounded functions f_j, as in , rather than in the more general case of functions bounded by a pseudorandom measure. It is clear from the proof that, in this more restricted setting, the kappa(rho) term that appears in the statement may be replaced by a polynomial dependence, and the o_rho(1) term may be bounded above by rho^-O(1)N^-Omega(1). This settles Theorem , where s is the Cauchy-Schwarz complexity of some system of forms (psi_1,dots,psi_d) that parametrises ker S. But s is at most d-2, as any system of d forms with finite Cauchy-Schwarz complexity has Cauchy-Schwarz complexity at most d-2. Therefore Theorem is proved.

Let $L$ be as in Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3}, and assume that $L$ has rational dimension $m$ and rational complexity at most $C$. Let $\Theta:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be some linear isomorphism satisfying $\Theta L(\mathbb{Z}^d) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^m$ and $\Vert \Theta \Vert_\infty \leqslant C$. Let $M$ be a rank matrix of $L$ (Proposition \ref{rank matrix}). Then the matrix $M^{-1}L$ satisfies $\Vert M^{-1} L\Vert_\infty \ll_{c,C} 1$ and has rational dimension $m$, since \\$((\Theta M )\circ (M^{-1}L))(\mathbb{Z}^d) = \Theta L(\mathbb{Z}^d) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^m$. The matrix $M^{-1}L$ also has rational complexity $O_{c,C}(1)$. Therefore, replacing $L$ with $M^{-1} L$, we may assume that the first $m$ columns of $L$ form the identity matrix.

As in Lemma \ref{Lemma full rational dimension}, we write $\Theta L = S$, where $S$ has integer coefficients and $\Vert \Theta \Vert_\infty \ll_{c,C} 1$. Hence $\Vert S\Vert_\infty \ll_{c,C}1$. But $\Theta$ must also have integer coefficients, as the first $m$ columns of $L$ form the identity matrix, and hence $\Vert \Theta^{-1} \Vert _\infty \ll_{c,C} 1$ as well. Note finally that $S \notin V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d)$, since $L \notin V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d)$.

Now, suppose that $G:\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow [0,1]$ is the indicator function of some convex domain $D$, with $D \subseteq [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]^m$.  \begin{equation}
 T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d) = \sum\limits_{\mathbf{r} \in R} \sum\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{n} \in [N]^d \\ S\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{r}}}  \prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j) \ll_{c,C,\varepsilon} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_{\rho}(1)
\end{equation}

Let $m,d,h$ be natural numbers satisfying $d\geqslant h\geqslant m+2$. Let $\mathbf{e_1}, \dots,\mathbf{e_d}$ denote the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $\mathbf{e_1}^\ast, \dots,\mathbf{e_d}^\ast$ denote the dual basis of $(\mathbb{R}^d)^\ast$. Then let $V^*_{\operatorname{degen},2}(m,d,h)$ denote the set of all pairs of linear maps $\Xi:\mathbb{R}^h \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ and $L:\mathbb{R}^h \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ for which there exist two indices $i,j \leqslant d$, and some real number $\lambda$, such that $(\mathbf{e_i}^* - \lambda \mathbf{e_j}^*)$ is non-zero and $\Xi^*(\mathbf{e_i}^* - \lambda \mathbf{e_j}^*) \in L^*((\mathbb{R}^m)^*)$. We call $V^*_{\operatorname{degen},2}(m,d,h)$ the \emph{dual pair degeneracy variety}.

\label{Lemma parametrising the image lattice}
Let $u,d$ be integers with $d\geqslant u+1$. Let $S:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^u$ be a surjective linear map with $S(\mathbb{Z}^d) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^u$, and suppose that $\Vert S\Vert_\infty \leqslant C$. Then there exists a set $\{\mathbf{a_1},\dots,\mathbf{a_u}\}\subset \mathbb{Z}^u$ that is a basis for the lattice $S(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ and for which $\Vert \mathbf{a_i}\Vert_\infty = O_C(1)$ for every $i$. Furthermore there exist $\mathbf{x_1},\dots,\mathbf{x_u}\in\mathbb{Z}^d$ such that, for every $i$, $S(\mathbf{x_i}) = \mathbf{a_i}$ and $\Vert \mathbf{x_i}\Vert_\infty = O_{C}(1)$.

nodes.statement: The lattice S(Z^d) is u dimensional, as S is surjective. If \ e_j:jleqslant d\ denotes the standard basis of R^d then integer combinations of elements from the set \S(e_j):jleqslant d\ span S(Z^d). Since Vert SVert_infty leqslant C, these vectors also satisfy Vert S(e_j)Vert_infty = O_C(1). Therefore the u successive minima of the lattice S(Z^d) are all O_C(1), and so, by Mahler's theorem () the lattice S(Z^d) has a basis \a_1,dots,a_u\ of the required form. Note that S has integer coefficients. The construction of suitable x_1,dots,x_u may be achieved by applying any of the standard algorithms. For example, using Gaussian elimination one may find a basis for ker S that, by inspection of the algorithm, consists of vectors with rational coordinates of naive height O_C(1). By clearing denominators, one gets vectors v_1,dots,v_d-u in Z^d whose integer span is a full-dimensional sublattice of the d-u dimensional lattice Z^d cap ker S, and that satisfy Vert v_iVert_infty = O_C(1) for all i. Now given some a_i, by its construction there must be some x_i in Z^d that satisfies S(x_i) = a_i. Write x_i = x_i|_ker S + x_i |_(ker S)^perp as the sum of the obvious projections. \label{Lemma replacing F cut-off}
Assume the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3} (in particular let $F$ be the indicator function $1_{[1,N]^d}$), and let $\sigma_F$ be any parameter in the range $0<\sigma_F<1/2$. Then there exists a Lipschitz function $F_{1,\sigma_F}:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow [0,1]$, supported on $[-2N,2N]^d$ and with Lipschitz constant $O(1/\sigma_FN)$, such that \[\vert T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert \ll \vert T_{F_{1,\sigma_F},G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert + O_{c,C}(\sigma_F).\]

Then there exists a Lipschitz function F_1,sigma_F:R^d longrightarrow [0,1], supported on [-2N,2N]^d and with Lipschitz constant O(1/sigma_FN), such that \[vert T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d)vert ll vert T_F_1,sigma_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d)vert + O_c,C(sigma_F).\]

Moreover, F_2,sigma_F is supported on \[ \x in R^d: dist(x, partial ([1,N]^d)) = O(sigma_F N)\.\] Therefore \[T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d) ll vert T_F_1,sigma_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d)vert + vert T_F_2,sigma_F,G,N^L(1,dots,1)vert.\] Therefore, since dist(L,V_rank^unif(m,d)) geqslant c, by Lemma we have \[vert T_F_2,sigma_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d)vert = O_c,C(sigma_F).\] This gives the lemma.

By Lemma \ref{Lipschitz approximation of convex cutoffs}, for any parameter $\sigma_F$ in the range $0< \sigma_F < 1/2$ we may write \[ 1_{[1,N]^d} = F_{1,\sigma_F} + O(F_{2,\sigma_F}),\] where $F_{1,\sigma_F},F_{2,\sigma_F}$ are Lipschitz functions supported on $[-2N,2N]^d$, with Lipschitz constants $O(1/\sigma_FN)$, and with $\int_\mathbf{x} F_{2,\sigma_F}(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x} = O(\sigma_F N^d)$. Moreover, $F_{2,\sigma_F}$ is supported on \[ \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d: \operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{x}, \partial ([1,N]^d)) = O(\sigma_F N)\}.\] 

Therefore \[T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d) \ll \vert T_{F_{1,\sigma_F},G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert + \vert T_{F_{2,\sigma_F},G,N}^L(1,\dots,1)\vert.\] Therefore, since $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)) \geqslant c$, by Lemma \ref{Lemma slightly less crude bound on number of solutions} we have \[\vert T_{F_{2,\sigma_F},G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert = O_{c,C}(\sigma_F).\] This gives the lemma.

nodes.statement: First we note that the lemma is obvious when u=0, since one may take Xi:R^d longrightarrow R^d to be the identity map, widetilder to be 0, and L^prime to be L. So assume that u > 1.\\ We proceed with a general reduction, familiar from our proof of Proposition , in which we may assume that the first m columns of L form the identity matrix. Indeed, let Theta:R^mlongrightarrow R^u be a rational map for L with Vert Theta Vert_infty leqslant C. Now let widetildeL : = M^-1 L, where M is a rank matrix of L (Proposition ), which, without loss of generality, consists of the first m columns of L. Let widetildeTheta : = Theta M and let widetildeG: = Gcirc M. Then \[ T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d) = T_F,widetildeG,N ^widetildeL(f_1,dots,f_d),\] and, considering widetildeTheta, widetildeL has rational complexity O_c,C(1). Furthermore, widetildeG is the indicator function of a convex domain contained in [-O_c,C(varepsilon), O_c,C(varepsilon)]^m. We also have dist(widetildeL,V_degen^*(m,d)) = Omega_c,C(1). Finally, for all tau_1,tau_2 in (0,1], we have that\\ A_widetildeL(tau_1,tau_2) asymp_c,C A_L(Omega_c,C(tau_1),Omega_c,C(tau_2)). Therefore, by replacing L with widetildeL and G with widetildeG, we may assume throughout the proof of Lemma that the first m columns of L form the identity matrix. This is at the cost of replacing varepsilon by O_c,C(varepsilon), C by O_c,C(1), and c by Omega_c,C(1). \\ Now let Theta:R^mlongrightarrow R^u be a rational map for L with Vert Theta Vert_infty = O_c,C(1). Since the first m columns of L form the identity matrix, Theta must have integer coefficients. \\ Part (1): By rank-nullity ker (Theta L) is a d-u dimensional subspace of R^d. The matrix of Theta L has integer coefficients and Vert Theta L Vert_infty = O_c,C(1). Combining these two facts, we see that ker (Theta L) cap Z^d is a d-u dimensional lattice, and by the standard algorithms one can find a lattice basis v^(1),dots, v^(d-u) in Z^d that satisfies Vert v^(i)Vert_infty = O_c,C(1) for every i. Define Xi:R^d-u longrightarrow R^d by \[ Xi(w):= sumlimits_i=1^d-u w_i v^(i).\] Then Xi satisfies property (1) of the lemma. Note that image of the map LXi:R^d-u longrightarrow R^m is exactly ker Theta. \\ Part (2): Since Vert Theta Vert_infty = O_c,C(1), if y inR^m and Theta(y) = r then Vert y Vert_infty gg_c,C Vertr Vert_infty. Recall that the support of G is contained within [-O_c,C,varepsilon(1),O_c,C,varepsilon(1)]^m, and that Theta L(Z^d) subseteq Z^u. It follows that there are at most O_c,C,varepsilon(1) possible vectors r in Z^u for which there exists a vector n inZ^d for which both G(Ln) neq 0 and Theta L n = r. Let R denote the set of all such vectors r. For each r in R, there exists a vector widetilderin Z^d such that Theta L widetilder = r and Vert widetilder Vert_infty = O_c,C,varepsilon(1). Let widetildeR denote the set of these widetilder. Then widetildeR satisfies part (2).\\ Before proceeding to prove part (3) of the lemma, we pause to apply Lemmas and . Indeed, applying these lemmas to the map S: = Theta L, there exists a set \ a_1,dots,a_u\ subset Z^u that is a basis for the lattice Theta L(Z^d) and for which Vert a_iVert_infty = O_c,C(1) for each i. Also, there exists a set of vectors \ x_1,dots,x_u\ subset Z^d such that Theta L(x_i)= a_i for each i, and Vert x_iVert_infty = O_c,C(1). By Lemma , B: = \x_i:ileqslant u\ cup \ Xi(w_j):jleqslant d-u\ is a basis for R^d and a lattice basis for Z^d, where w_1,dots,w_d-u denotes the standard basis of R^d-u.\\ Part (3): By the definition of widetildeR, and the fact that Xi(Z^d-u) = Z^d cap ker (Theta L), we have T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d) = sumlimits_widetilder in widetildeRfrac1N^d-m sumlimits_n in Z^d-u Big(prodlimits_j=1^d f_j(xi_j(n) + widetilder_j) Big)F(Xi(n) + widetilder) G(LXi(n) + Lwidetilder), where widetilder_j denotes the j^th coordinates of widetilder. Now by an easy linear algebraic argument (recorded in Lemma ), R^m = span(Lx_i:ileqslant u) oplus ker Theta as an algebraic direct sum, and there exists an invertible linear map P:R^m longrightarrow R^m such that P((span(Lx_i:ileqslant u))) &= R^u times \0\^m-u, \\ P(ker Theta) &= \0\^u times R^m-u, and both Vert PVert_infty = O_c,C(1) and Vert P^-1 Vert_infty = O_c,C(1). We have \[ G(LXi(n) + Lwidetilder) = (G circ P^-1)(PLXi(n) + PLwidetilder),\] and we note that PLXi(n) in \0\^u times R^m-u for every n in Z^d-u. Define G_widetilder:R^m-u longrightarrow [0,1] by \[G_widetilder(x) : = (Gcirc P^-1)(x_0 + PLwidetilder),\] where x_0 is the extension of x by 0 in the first u coordinates. Then the function G_widetilder is the indicator function of a convex set contained in [-O_c,C,varepsilon(1),O_c,C,varepsilon(1)]^m-u. Define \[F_widetilder(n) : = F(Xi(n) + widetilder).\] Then F_widetilder has Lipschitz constant O_c,C(1/sigma_F N) and F_widetilder is supported on \\[-O_c,C,varepsilon(N),O_c,C,varepsilon(N)]^d-u. (For a full proof of this fact, apply Lemma to the map Xi). So F_widetilder and G_widetilder satisfy part (3).\\ Part (4): Writing pi_m-u:R^mlongrightarrow R^m-u for the projection onto the final m-u coordinates, expression () is equal to sumlimits_widetilder in widetildeRfrac1N^d-m sumlimits_n in Z^d-u Big(prodlimits_j=1^d f_j(xi_j(n) + widetilder_j) Big)F_widetilder(n)G_widetilder( pi_m-u PLXi(n)). Let L^prime: = pi_m-u PLXi. Then L^prime:R^d-u longrightarrow R^m-u is surjective, and \[T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d) = sumlimits_widetilder in widetildeRT_F_widetilder,G_widetilder,N^L^prime,Xi,widetilder(f_1,dots,f_d).\] This resolves part (4).\\ Part (5): We wish to show that L^prime is purely irrational. Suppose for contradiction that there exists some surjective linear map varphi:R^m-u longrightarrow R with varphi L^prime (Z^d-u) subseteq Z, i.e. with varphi pi_m-u PLXi(Z^d-u) subseteq Z. Then define the map Theta^prime:R^m longrightarrow R^u+1 by \[ Theta^prime(x) : = (Theta(x),varphi pi_m-u P(x)).\] Then Theta^prime is surjective, and Theta^prime L(Z^d)subseteq Z^u+1. (This second fact is immediately seen by writing Z^d with respect to the lattice basis B from ()). This contradicts the assumption that L has rational dimension u. So L^prime is purely irrational. \\ Part (6): The bound Vert L^primeVert_infty = O_c,C(1) follows immediately from the bounds on the coefficients of Xi, L, P, and pi_m-u separately. We wish to prove that dist(L^prime, V_rank(m-u,d-u)) gg_c,C 1, i.e. that\\ dist(pi_m-u PLXi, V_rank(m-u,d-u)) gg_c,C 1. Suppose for contradiction that, for a small parameter eta, there exists a linear map Q: R^d-u longrightarrow R^m-u such that Vert QVert_infty<eta and pi_m-u PLXi + Q has rank less than m-u. Recall that PLXi (R^d-u) = \0\^u times R^m-u. So, extending Q by zeros to a map Q:R^d-u longrightarrow \0\^u times R^m-u, and applying P^-1, there is a map Q^prime:R^d-u longrightarrow R^m such that Vert Q^primeVert_infty=O_c,C(eta) and LXi + Q^prime has rank less than m-u. We may factorise Q^prime = HXi for some m-by-d matrix H. Indeed let \[B := \ x_i: ileqslant u\ cup \Xi(w_j): jleqslant d-u\\] be the basis of R^d from (), i.e. the basis formed by applying Lemma to the map S: = Theta L. Define the linear map H by H(Xi(w_j)): = Q^prime(w_j) for each j and H(x_i): = 0 for each i. Since the change of basis matrix between B and the standard basis of R^d has integer coefficients with absolute values at most O_c,C(1), it follows that the matrix representing H with respect to the standard bases satisfies Vert HVert_infty = O_c,C(eta). So we know that (L+H)Xi has rank less than m-u. But Xi:R^d-u longrightarrow R^d is injective, so this implies that the rank of L+H is less than m. Hence dist(L,V_rank(m,d)) = O_c,C(eta), which contradicts the assumptions of the lemma (if eta is small enough). So dist(L^prime,V_rank(m-u,d-u)) gg_c,C 1 as required. \\ Part (7): We wish to show that dist((Xi,L^prime),V_degen,2^*(m-u,d,d-u)) = Omega_c,C(1). Suppose for contradiction that, for a small parameter eta, there exists a linear map Q:R^d-u longrightarrow R^d such that Vert QVert_infty leqslant eta and dist((Xi + Q, L^prime ),V_degen,2^*(m-u,d,d-u)) leqslant eta. In other words, we suppose there exist two indices i,jleqslant d, and a real number lambda, such that e_i^* - lambdae_j^* is non-zero and \[ (Xi + Q)^*(e_i^* - lambdae_j^*) in (L^prime)^*((R^m-u)^*),\] where \e_1,dots,e_d\ denotes the standard basis of R^d and \e_1^*,dots,e_d^*\ denotes the dual basis. Expanding out the definition of L^prime, this means that there exists some varphi in (R^m-u)^* such that \[Xi^*(e_i^* - lambdae_j^* - L^*(P^* pi_m-u^*(varphi))) = -Q^*(e_i^* - lambdae_j^*).\] Because Vert QVert_infty leqslant eta, this means that Vert Xi^*(e_i^* - lambdae_j^* - L^*(P^* pi_m-u^*(varphi)))Vert_infty = O(eta). Let B^* := \ x_i^*: ileqslant u\ cup \Xi(w_j)^*: jleqslant d-u\ denote the basis of (R^d)^* that is dual to the basis B from (). It follows from part (4) of Lemma and () that \[e_i^* - lambdae_j^* - L^*(P^* pi_m-u^*(varphi)) = omega_V + omega_W,\] where omega_V in L^* Theta^*((R^u)^*), omega_W in span(Xi(w_j)^*:jleqslant d-u), and Vertomega_WVert_infty = O_c,C(eta). nodes.name: $\eta$-supported
nodes.statement: Let chi:Rlongrightarrow [0,1] be a measurable function, and let eta be a positive parameter. We say that chi is eta-supported if chi is supported on [-eta,eta] and chi(x) equiv 1 for all xin [-eta/2,eta/2].
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{Defintion eta supported}
Let $\chi:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow [0,1]$ be a measurable function, and let $\eta$ be a positive parameter. We say that $\chi$ is \emph{$\eta$-supported} if $\chi$ is supported on $[-\eta,\eta]$ and $\chi(x) \equiv 1$ for all $x\in [-\eta/2,\eta/2]$.

\label{Lemma non quantitative equivalence of degeneracies}
Let $m,d,h$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant h\geqslant  m+2$. Let $\Xi:\mathbb{R}^h\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ be an injective linear map, let $L:\mathbb{R}^h\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and suppose that $(\Xi,L)\notin V^*_{\operatorname{degen},2}(m,d,h)$. Let $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{h-m}\longrightarrow \ker L$ be any surjective linear map. Then the linear map $\Xi \Phi:\mathbb{R}^{h-m} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$, viewed as a system of homogenous linear forms, is not in $V_{\operatorname{degen}}(h-m,d)$.

But then Phi(R^h-m) subset ker (Xi^*(e_i^* - lambda e_j^*)), i.e. Xi^*(e_i^* - lambda e_j^*) in (ker L)^0. But (ker L)^0 = L^*((R^m)^*), and so Xi^*(e_i^* - lambda e_j^*) in L^*((R^m)^*). Then, by the definition of V_degen,2^*(m,d,h), we have (Xi,L)in V^*_degen,2(m,d,h), which is a contradiction.

\label{Quantitative orthonormal basis parametrisation}
Let $m,d,h$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant h\geqslant m+2$, and let $c,C$ be positive constants. Let $\Xi:\mathbb{R}^h \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ be a linear map, and let $L:\mathbb{R}^h \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map. Suppose that $\Vert \Xi\Vert_\infty \leqslant C$, and $\operatorname{dist}((\Xi,L),V^*_{\operatorname{degen},2}(m,d,h))\geqslant c$. Let $K$ denote $\ker L$, choose any orthonormal basis $\{\mathbf{v^{(1)}},\dots, \mathbf{v^{(h-m)}}\}$ for $K$, and let $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{h-m}\longrightarrow K$ denote the associated parametrisation, i.e. $\Phi(\mathbf{x}) := \sum_{i=1}^{h-m}x_i\mathbf{v^{(i)}}$. Then $\Vert \Xi  \Phi\Vert_{\infty} = O(C)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\Xi\Phi, V_{\operatorname{degen}}(h-m,d)) = \Omega(c)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem \ref{Converse to main theorem}
nodes.statement: Recall the hypotheses of Theorem . In particular, we suppose that liminflimits_Nrightarrowinftydist(L,V^*_degen(m,d)) = 0, i.e. we assume that dist(L,V_degen^*(m,d)) = omega(N)^-1, for some function omega(N) such that limsup_Nrightarrowinfty omega(N) = infty. Let eta be a small positive quantity, picked small enough in terms of c and C, and let N be a natural number that is large enough so that omega(N)geqslant eta^-1 and eta Ngeqslant max(1,varepsilon). All implied constants to follow will be independent of eta. Since F is the indicator function of [1,N]^d and G is the indicator function of [-varepsilon,varepsilon]^m, one has \[T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d) = frac1N^d-m sumlimits_substackn in [N]^d \\ Vert Ln Vert_infty leqslant varepsilon prodlimits_j=1^d f_j(n_j).\] Our aim is to construct functions f_1,dots,f_d:[N] longrightarrow [-1,1] such that \[ min_jVert f_jVert_U^s+1[N] leqslant rho\] for some rho at most 1 and that T_F,G,N^L(f_1,dots,f_d) > H(rho) + E_rho(N). We begin by observing that the condition Vert LnVert_inftyleqslant varepsilon implies certain constraints on two of the variables n_i. Indeed, let L^primein V_degen^*(m,d) be such that Vert L - L^prime Vert_infty = dist(L,V_degen^*(m,d)). Write lambda_ij for the coefficients of L and lambda_ij^prime for the coefficients of L^prime. By reordering columns, without loss of generality we may assume that there exist real numbers \a_i\_i=1^m not all 0 s.t. for all j in the range 3leqslant jleqslant d we have sumlimits_i=1^m a_i lambda^prime_ij = 0, and further we may assume that for all i we have lambda^prime_i1 = lambda_i1 and lambda^prime_i2 = lambda_i2 (else L^primein V_degen^*(m,d) is not one of the closest matrices to L). By reordering rows and rescaling, we may assume that a_1 has maximal absolute value amongst all the a_i, and that vert a_1vert = 1. Define b_1:=sumlimits_i=1^m a_i lambda_i1, b_2:= sumlimits_i=1^m a_i lambda_i2, and let nin [N]^d be some solution to Vert LnVert_infty leqslant varepsilon. The critical observation is that (), combined with the assumptions on the a_i, implies that vert b_1 n_1 + b_2n_2vert ll eta N. Indeed, for j in the range 3leqslant jleqslant d we have leftvertsumlimits_i=1^m a_ilambda_ijrightvert & = leftvertsumlimits_i=1^m a_i(lambda_ij - lambda^prime_ij)rightvert \\ &ll eta. Since Vert LnVert_infty leqslant varepsilon, we certainly have that leftvert b_1 n_1 + b_2n_2 + sumlimits_j=3^d n_jsumlimits_i=1^m a_i lambda_ijrightvert ll varepsilon, and then () follows by the triangle inequality and the fact that eta Ngeqslant varepsilon.\\ The constraint () will turn out to be enough for the proof. We consider various cases, constructing different counterexample functions f_1 and f_2 based on the size and sign of b_1 and b_2. To facilitate this, we let c_1 be a suitably small positive constant, depending on c and C, but independent of eta. All constants C_1 and C_2 to follow will be assumed to satisfy C_1,C_2 = O_c,C(1). \\\\ Case 1: vert b_1vert,vert b_2vert leqslant c_1. Under the assumptions of Theorem , this case is actually precluded. Indeed, consider the matrix L^primeprime, defined by taking lambda_ij^primeprime = lambda_ij^prime for all pairs (i.j)in [m]times[d], except for (1,1) and (1,2). In these cases we let lambda_11^primeprime &= lambda_11^prime - fracb_1a_1\\ lambda_12^primeprime & = lambda_12^prime - fracb_2a_1. Then sumlimits_i=1^m a_ilambda_ij^primeprime = 0 for all j in the range 1leqslant jleqslant d. In other words we have shown that Vert L-L^primeprimeVert_infty leqslant eta + c_1 for some matrix L^primeprime with rank less than m. Since eta + c_1< c (if c_1 is small enough), this implies that dist(L,V_rank(m,d))<c, which contradicts the assumptions of Theorem . Therefore this case is indeed precluded. \\ Case 2: b_1,b_2 both of the same sign, and b_1,b_2geqslant c_1. In this case, () impliesfootnoteThe same conclusion is true for n_2, but this will not be needed. that n_1leqslant C_1eta N for some constant C_1. Now, define f_1:[N]longrightarrow [-1,1] to be the indicator function of the interval [lceil C_1eta Nrceil, N]cap N. We then have Vert f_1 - 1Vert_U^s+1[N] &ll Big(frac1N^s+2 sumlimits_x,h_1,dots,h_s+1ll C_1eta N 1Big)^frac12^s+1\\ &leqslant C_2(C_1eta)^fracs+22^s+1 for some constant C_2. However, observe that vert T_F,G,N^L(f_1-1,1,dots,1)vert &= vert T_F,G,N^L(f_1,1,dots,1) - T_F,G,N^L(1,1,dots,1)vert\\ & = vert 0 - T_F,G,N^L(1,1,dots,1)vert gg_c,C,varepsilon 1 by the hypotheses of Theorem . If T_F,G,N^L(f_1 - 1,1,dots,1) did not satisfy (), then 1 ll_c,C,varepsilon H(rho) + E_rho(1), where rho := C_2(C_1eta)^fracs+22^s+1. Picking eta small enough, then N large enough, this inequality cannot possibly hold, and we have a contradiction. So T_F,G,N^L(f_1 - 1,1,dots,1) satisfies (). \\ Case 3: b_1,b_2 of opposite signs, and b_1,b_2geqslant c_1. This is the most involved case, although the central idea is very simple. The condition () confines n_2 to lie within a certain distance of a fixed multiple of n_1. By constructing functions f_1 and f_2 using random choices of blocks of this length, but coupled in such a way that condition () is very likely to hold, we can guarantee that T_F,G,N^L(f_1-p,f_2-p,1,dots,1) is bounded away from zero, where p is the probability used to choose the random blocks. However, despite the block construction and the coupling, the functions f_1 and f_2 still individually exhibit enough randomness to conclude that Vert f_1 - pVert _U^s+1[N] = o(1) as Nrightarrow infty, and the same for f_2. \\ We now fill in the technical details. \label{Proposition Gowers Cauchy Schwarz}
Let $d$ be a natural number, and, for each $\boldsymbol{\omega} \in \{0,1\}^d$, let $f_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}:[0,1]\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded measurable function. Define the Gowers inner-product \[\langle (f_{\boldsymbol{\omega}})_{\boldsymbol{\omega}\in \{0,1\}^d}\rangle :=  \int\limits_{(x,\mathbf{h}) \in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}} \prod\limits_{\boldsymbol{\omega} \in \{0,1\}^d}\mathcal{C}^{\vert \boldsymbol{\omega} \vert} f_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}(x+\sum\limits_{i=1}^d h_i\omega_i) \, dx\,dh_1\cdots dh_d.\] Then \[\vert\langle (f_{\boldsymbol{\omega}})_{\boldsymbol{\omega}\in \{0,1\}^d}\rangle \vert \leqslant \prod\limits_{\boldsymbol{\omega}\in \{0,1\}^d} \Vert f_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\Vert_{U^d(\mathbb{R})}.\]

nodes.name: Lipschitz functions
nodes.statement: We say that a function F:R^m longrightarrow C is Lipschitz, with Lipschitz constant at most M, if \[M geqslant suplimits_substackx,yin R^m \\ xneq y frac vert F(x) - F(y) vertVert x - y Vert_infty .\] We say that a function G:R^m/Z^m longrightarrow C is Lipschitz, with Lipschitz constant at most M, if \[ M geqslant suplimits_substackx,yin R^m/Z^m \\ xneq y frac vert G(x) - G(y) vertVert x - y Vert_R^m/Z^m.\]
nodes.raw_latex:
We say that a function $F:\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is Lipschitz, with Lipschitz constant at most $M$, if \[M \geqslant \sup\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb{R}^m \\ \mathbf{x}\neq \mathbf{y}}} \frac{ \vert F(\mathbf{x}) - F(\mathbf{y}) \vert}{\Vert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y} \Vert_\infty }.\]

We say that a function $G:\mathbb{R}^m/\mathbb{Z}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is Lipschitz, with Lipschitz constant at most $M$, if \[ M \geqslant \sup\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb{R}^m/\mathbb{Z}^m \\ \mathbf{x}\neq \mathbf{y}}} \frac{ \vert G(\mathbf{x}) - G(\mathbf{y}) \vert}{\Vert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y} \Vert_{\mathbb{R}^m/\mathbb{Z}^m}}.\]

\label{Lipschitz approximation of convex cutoffs}
Let $N$ be a positive real, let $m$ be a natural number, let $K$ be a convex subset of $[-N,N]^m$, and let $\sigma$ be some parameter in the range $0<\sigma<1/2$. Then there exist Lipschitz functions $F_\sigma, G_\sigma:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow [0,1]$ supported on $[-2N,2N]^m$, both with Lipschitz constant at most $O(\frac{1}{\sigma N})$, such that \[1_K = F_\sigma + O(G_\sigma)\] and $\int_{\mathbf{x}} G_\sigma(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x} = O(\sigma N^m)$. Furthermore, $F_\sigma(\mathbf{x})\geqslant 1_K(\mathbf{x})$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^m$, and $G$ is supported on $\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m: \operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{x},\partial(K)) \leqslant \sigma N\}$.

nodes.name: \textbf{Proof of \emph{Proposition \ref{rank matrix}}}
nodes.statement: Let k be equal to left( d\\ mright), and identify R^md with the space of m-by-d real matrices. Then let f_1,dots,f_k be the k polynomials on R^md that are given by the k determinants of m-by-m submatrices of L. One then sees that V_rank(m,d) is exactly the set of common zeros of the functions f_i. This is since row rank equals column rank, and linear independence of columns in a square matrix can be detected by the determinant. Since we assume that Vert LVert_inftyleqslant C and dist(L,V_rank(m,d))geqslant c we can fruitfully apply Proposition to deduce that there is some j for which vert f_j(L)vert= Omega_c,C(1). The matrix M whose determinant corresponds to the polynomial f_j is exactly the claimed rank matrix. \\ This settles the first part of Proposition . The second part then follows immediate by the construction of M^-1 as the adjugate matrix of M divided by det M. \\ The third part, namely the statement about linear combinations of rows, follows quickly from the others. Indeed, without loss of generality, assume that the rank matrix M is realised by columns 1 through m. Then, the fact that the rows of L are linearly independent means that there are unique real numbers a_i such that sumlimits_i=1^m a_i lambda_ij = v_j for all j in the range 1leqslant jleqslant d. (Recall that (lambda_ij)_ileqslant m,jleqslant d denotes the coefficients of L). Restricting to j in the range 1leqslant j leqslant m, we observe that the a_i are forced to satisfy left( a_1 \\ vdots \\ a_m right) = (M^T)^-1left( v_1 \\ vdots \\ v_m right). Since Vert (M^-1)^TVert_infty = Vert M^-1Vert_infty = O_c,C(1), we conclude that a_i = O_c,C,C_1(1) for all i. \\ The final part of the proposition is to show that if dist(L,V_rank^unif(m,d))geqslant c then, for each j, there exists a rank matrix of L that doesn't include the j^th column. But this statement follows immediately from the above, after having deleted the j^th column.

Since we assume that $\Vert L\Vert_\infty\leqslant C$ and $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d))\geqslant c$ we can fruitfully apply Proposition \ref{sec.Analysis algebra quant} to deduce that there is some $j$ for which $\vert f_j(L)\vert= \Omega_{c,C}(1)$. The matrix $M$ whose determinant corresponds to the polynomial $f_j$ is exactly the claimed rank matrix. \\

This settles the first part of Proposition \ref{rank matrix}. The second part then follows immediate by the construction of $M^{-1}$ as the adjugate matrix of $M$ divided by $\det M$. \\

The third part, namely the statement about linear combinations of rows, follows quickly from the others. Indeed, without loss of generality, assume that the rank matrix $M$ is realised by columns $1$ through $m$. Then, the fact that the rows of $L$ are linearly independent means that there are unique real numbers $a_i$ such that $\sum\limits_{i=1}^m a_i \lambda_{ij} = v_{j}$ for all $j$ in the range $1\leqslant j\leqslant d$. (Recall that $(\lambda_{ij})_{i\leqslant m,j\leqslant d}$ denotes the coefficients of $L$). Restricting to $j$ in the range $1\leqslant j \leqslant m$, we observe that the $a_i$ are forced to satisfy $$\left(\begin{matrix} 
a_1 \\ 
\vdots \\
a_m
\end{matrix}\right)
 = (M^{T})^{-1}\left(\begin{matrix} 
v_1 \\ 
\vdots \\
v_m
\end{matrix}\right).$$ Since $\Vert (M^{-1})^T\Vert_{\infty} = \Vert M^{-1}\Vert_{\infty} = O_{c,C}(1)$, we conclude that $a_i = O_{c,C,C_1}(1)$ for all $i$. \\

The final part of the proposition is to show that if $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d))\geqslant c$ then, for each $j$, there exists a rank matrix of $L$ that doesn't include the $j^{th}$ column. But this statement follows immediately from the above, after having deleted the $j^{th}$ column.

The partition $\mathcal{P}_i$ has $s_i+1$ parts, for some $s_i$ at most $s$.

Such a vector can be found using Gaussian elimination, say. Furthermore, $\psi_i^\prime (\mathbf{0},\mathbf{w})= w_1 + \cdots + w_{s+1}$. Also, $n^\prime = n+ s+1$, which is at most $n+m-1$. So Proposition \ref{normal form algorithm} is proved if for each $k$ we can find such a vector $\mathbf{f_k}$ that additionally satisfies $\Vert\mathbf{f_k}\Vert_\infty = O_{c_1,C_1}(1)$. 

Consider a fixed $k$, and let $\Gamma$ be the set of possible implementations of Gaussian elimination on the set of forms $\psi_i \cup \{\psi_j: j\in \mathcal{C}_k\}$ to find a solution vector $\mathbf{f_k}$. If in the course of implementing these algorithms we are given a free choice for a co-ordinate of $\mathbf{f_k}$, we set it to be equal to zero. Note that $\vert \Gamma\vert = O(1)$.

Let $\mathbf{b_1},\dots,\mathbf{b_m}$ denote the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^m$, and define $P$ by letting
\begin{align}
\label{definition of P}
P(L\mathbf{x_i}) &:= \mathbf{b_i}, \qquad \quad 1\leqslant i\leqslant u \nonumber \\
P(\mathbf{y_j}) &:= \mathbf{b_{j+u}}, \qquad 1\leqslant j\leqslant m-u,
\end{align}
\noindent and then extending linearly to all of $\mathbb{R}^m$. Clearly $P((\operatorname{span}(L\mathbf{x_i}:i\leqslant u))) = \mathbb{R}^u \times \{0\}^{m-u}$ and $P(\ker \Theta) = \{0\}^{u} \times \mathbb{R}^{m-u}$. If $L\mathbf{x_i}$ were all vectors with integer coordinates then this bound would be immediate as well, as then $P^{-1}$ would have integer coordinates and hence $\vert \det P^{-1}\vert \geqslant 1$. As it is, we have to proceed more slowly.
